1	# Growth — extract lessons (per repo)
2	
3	The growth lifecycle's capture stage, over **both** lesson sources in one run: the window's repo activity
4	(commits, merged PRs, issue discussion) and the conversation logs captured from working sessions. Each
5	durable, reusable lesson is folded into the repo's own **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/` — the
6	normalized capture surface) at the repo's own level, without straining to generalize it. The run lands its
7	edits through a single PR **delivered to land** (on the default delivery settings it merges once the repo's
8	checks pass, with no human review — daily capture never piles up as review requests); finding nothing to add
9	on a given run is a perfectly good outcome.
10	
11	You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue whose **Context section is binding
12	scope**: it names which halves are live, the substantive commit shas and the PRs/issues touched in the
13	window, and whether the retention prune is due. That is the work; do not widen it.
14	
15	> This is the **unattended daily** capture. It writes only the repo's *own* local packs, so — **unlike** an
16	> owner-requested, in-session retrospective (which delivers a PR for a human to review) — it opens a PR and
17	> **delivers it to land** (the shared procedure under *Output* below; on the default settings GitHub lands it
18	> once the repo's checks pass). The shared canon stays human-gated — lifting anything up into it is the
19	> central promote task's job (canon-side), and that PR waits for the owner.
20	
21	## Conventions used in this doc
22	
23	- **Default branch.** `main` stands for **this repository's default branch** — substitute whatever the repo uses.
24	- **Access split — local git for repo content, MCP for the issue/PR API.** The repo's own content is plain
25	  **local git** in the checkout: the commits, the `conversation-logs` branch and its files
26	  (`git fetch`/`show`/`rm`/`push`), and staging the lesson edits onto a branch. Reading issue/PR activity,
27	  opening the PR and delivering it, posting the exchange summaries and the tracking-issue log go
28	  through the session's **GitHub MCP tools** (`mcp__github__*`). The unattended run has no shell GitHub
29	  access — the shell reaches only a git-over-HTTPS proxy scoped to one repo, with no REST credential — so
30	  never reach for `gh`/`curl` or a cross-repo clone.
31	- **The repo's local packs.** The set identified in
32	  [this pack's README](../../README.md#identifying-a-projects-capture-surface-its-local-packs) — everything
33	  under `.claudinite/local/packs/` (the legacy `.claudinite/local_packs/` accepted during the rename
34	  window), the repo's own packs; never the read-only mounted canon elsewhere under `.claudinite/`.
35	
36	## The run — two source skills, then the upgrade pass
37	
38	The **method** for each source lives in its skill; this worker only frames the run around them. Don't
39	re-derive any of it here.
40	
41	1. **Activity half — the [extract-from-activity](../../skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) skill**, over
42	   exactly the commits, merged PRs and issues named in Context. **Skip this half entirely when Context says
43	   the activity half is not in scope** (a quiet repo whose only reason to run was the retention prune).
44	2. **Conversation half — the [extract-from-conversations](../../skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md)
45	   skill**, over the repo's captured logs. `git fetch origin conversation-logs`, then list its files
46	   (`git ls-tree --name-only origin/conversation-logs`); no branch, or no `*.jsonl`, and this half is done.
47	   Give each log captured in the recent window a **fresh pass** (its filename carries the capture stamp;
48	   corpus dedup makes an overlapping re-read harmless, so err toward re-reading the last several days), and
49	   post the skill's provenance summary for each rule that actually lands.
50	3. **Retention prune**, when Context says it is due. Read `retention_days` from this repo's
51	   `.claudinite-checks.json` (the grow_with_claudinite entry's `config.retention_days`) — unset means this
52	   step is skipped entirely (capture-only adoption). For each log whose filename stamp is older than
53	   `retention_days` days: give it the **final hindsight pass** the skill describes (anything it still yields
54	   lands like any other keeper), then `git rm` it on the `conversation-logs` branch and push (commit message
55	   ending `[skip ci]`). The branch is never merged and its history is never rewritten — plain add/remove
56	   commits only. This push to the non-default logs branch is outside the outcome taxonomy (DESIGN §1).
57	4. **Upgrade pass — the [prose-to-checks](../../skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md) skill, over what *this run*
58	   just wrote.** Both halves route down the local promotion ladder as they go, but a lesson written as prose
59	   under time pressure is exactly where a convertible rule hides. So before opening the PR, take the prose
60	   this run added and ask the skill's questions of it: does it clear the working-rule gate, and does it
61	   constrain a static signature a check could observe? If yes, convert it now — author the rule module,
62	   register it in its pack's `pack.mjs`, prove it with a **see-it-fail** fixture, and apply the deletion
63	   test to the prose the check now stands beside. **Scope is this run's own additions only** — the standing
64	   prose backlog is the weekly [prose-to-checks-sweep](../prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md)'s job, and widening
65	   into it here would duplicate that task's work under an auto-merging PR.
66	
67	If an edit touches something a test reads (a doc constant, a code path), run the repo's offline test suite
68	and keep it green before opening the PR.
69	
70	## Output: one PR, delivered to land

# Extract lessons from repo activity

The **artifact** half of lesson extraction: mine what a window of work left behind — commits, the PRs
merged in it, the issue discussion around them — for durable, reusable lessons, and fold each into the
repo's **own local packs**. Its sibling [extract-from-conversations](../extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md)
mines the *dialogue*; this one never sees a conversation, only what the work committed.

The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
surface lives are shared with that sibling and stay canonical in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't re-derive it. What follows is only
what reading *artifacts* adds.

## Capture at the repo's own level

Write each lesson at whatever level reads naturally for this repo — refer to its files, services, or
mechanics wherever that's what makes the lesson clear. Don't force either extreme: don't contort a lesson
to be hyper-specific, and don't polish it into a general, portable rule. Making a lesson portable is the
growth lifecycle's **promote** stage, done canon-side later over whatever merged here; here, just capture
it usefully and let promotion lift whatever turns out to travel.

## Read the window — and read merged PRs properly

Work only the window you were handed (a scheduled run gets it as binding scope in the dispatch issue's
Context; an owner's ask names it in words). Never widen it.

1. **The commits** — full bodies, and the diff wherever a fix is non-obvious.
2. **The PRs merged in the window** — read these *first* and read them *whole*: the diff **and** the
   review discussion. A merged PR is usually the window's richest lesson source, because it records what
   was tried, what a reviewer pushed back on, and why the landed shape won. A verdict reached in review
   is a lesson already argued; the commit alone shows only the winner.
3. **The issue activity** it names — the comments changed on those numbers.

## What artifacts signal — and what they don't

The signals worth converting here are the ones an artifact can carry: a fix whose diff is small but whose
*reason* is not obvious from the code; a review comment that names a convention the author missed; a
revert or a follow-up fix that says the first shape was wrong; a PR that grew several rounds because its
approach was re-decided mid-flight.

**An already-settled, already-enforced implementation choice is not a lesson.** If a check or a test
already pins the shape — which roots a CI sweep walks, which contract a construction must satisfy — and
all that is left to say is *why it looks like that*, that explanation belongs as a comment at the
implementation site, not as prose in a pack. A rule earns its place by steering a **future** decision or
catching a **repeatable** mistake, not by narrating a past one that is already locked in.

Wall-time and dialogue friction (a clarifying round-trip, a backtrack, a wait sat through) leave no trace
in a diff. Don't infer them from artifacts — that is the conversation sibling's territory, working from
logs that actually carry the timestamps.

## Landing it

Route each keeper down the ladder in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — check first,
then pack skill, prose last — into the local pack whose territory owns it. Write more checks and less
prose, and keep each addition terse and in the repo's own voice.

A new check ships **green or not at all**: see it fail on a violating fixture and pass on a clean one. A
rule that cannot be made confident lands as prose instead — never as a broken check.

Finding nothing is a perfectly good and common outcome; a duplicate or invented "lesson" is worse than
adding nothing.

# Extract lessons from a conversation

The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.

The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.

## The goal

Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.

## Where the conversation comes from

- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.

**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
when a session is done enough to mine.

## What to look for — the friction signals

Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.

### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user

The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.

**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
correctly **without the round-trip**.

### 2. Suboptimal agent actions

The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
convention and had it corrected in review.

**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
first, not after a detour.

### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them

The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.

**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
was already optimal.

**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
loss of quality.

## Encode the questions the user keeps asking

The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.

## Two passes per log, and the second one may overturn the first

A captured log gets a **fresh pass** within a day of capture and a **final hindsight pass** just before
retention deletes it, against the corpus as it stands by then. The hindsight pass is a real re-read, not a
formality: a friction signal that looked situational the first time may have recurred since, and a lesson
landed since may have made a keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes.

## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it

For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):

- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.

**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
silence it replaced.

1	########## .claudinite/local/packs/browser-speech/RULES.md
2	# Browser speech — the judgment core
3	
4	Driving the browser's speech surfaces (`SpeechRecognition` / `webkitSpeechRecognition`,
5	`chrome.tts`, `speechSynthesis`, the mic capture behind them). The mechanical rules — completion
6	handlers, mic release, which constraints a mic capture may even ask for, whether an error mapping
7	is total, and whether interim hypotheses are gated before delivery — are this pack's six checks;
8	what follows is only what no check can decide for you.
9	
10	Each rule below is a judgment about the API, and holds for any voice-driven app. Where one cites
11	this repo — a file, a decision record, a measured number — that is the **evidence** it was drawn
12	from, not the scope it applies to; a rule grounded in a real instance beats one asserted in the
13	abstract. The measured values (the pause window especially) are this product's and should be
14	re-measured elsewhere, not copied.
15	
16	The one thing to keep in mind everywhere below: **speech failures are silent**. Nothing throws,
17	nothing logs, the UI keeps showing a live session — the user just hears nothing, or is heard by
18	nobody. Design each of these surfaces so every path produces exactly one observable outcome.
19	
20	## Where each API can run
21	
22	- `chrome.tts` is **not exposed to content scripts**. The session lives in the page (speech
23	  recognition needs a document, and the mic grant belongs to nytimes.com), so speaking is a
24	  relay: the content script sends `cc:speak` over the long-lived `cc-session` port and the
25	  service worker calls `chrome.tts` — `speech/remote-tts-port.js` presents the same contract as
26	  `speech/tts-port.js` so the orchestrator can't tell the difference. Prefer `chrome.tts` over
27	  `speechSynthesis` because it is immune to the page's autoplay rules (decision D2).
28	
29	## Self-echo is an application problem, not a constraints problem
30	
31	`webkitSpeechRecognition` **owns its own capture and exposes no hook for
32	`MediaTrackConstraints`** — you cannot ask the recognizer for echo cancellation. Chrome applies
33	its default AEC (a loopback of playout audio) to that capture, which already attenuates
34	`speechSynthesis`, but it misses `chrome.tts`'s OS-rendered output. So the residual echo is
35	handled at the app level by a string-match echo guard (REQ-SPCH-005), and that is the design,
36	not a stopgap (decision D11).
37	
38	Two traps around this:
39	
40	- `suppressLocalAudioPlayback` and `restrictOwnAudio` read like the fix for this and are not:
41	  they are **`getDisplayMedia` screen-capture** constraints, filtering a captured tab's own
42	  playout out of that tab's track, and `getUserMedia` ignores them without a word. The cost of
43	  reaching for one is not the dead property — it is that the echo guard that would have worked
44	  never gets written. (Enforced by the `mic-constraints-not-screen-capture` check.)
45	- The constraints you *can* set (`echoCancellation`, `noiseSuppression`, `autoGainControl`)
46	  apply only to the one capture you own — the permission preflight.
47	
48	## Ask for the microphone in a moment you chose
49	
50	Surface the permission prompt deliberately, with a short warm-up `getUserMedia` — not as a side
51	effect of the first listen cycle. Two rules for that preflight:
52	
53	- **Run it even when permission is already granted.** Otherwise the device is only warmed, and
54	  AEC engagement only known, on the very first grant.
55	- **Retry once bare when the constrained call rejects.** A rejection is either a real denial or
56	  a browser balking at the constraint shape; only a second failure is a genuine denial. Reading
57	  a constraint quirk as "mic denied" ends the session for no reason.
58	
59	(The capture must then be released on every path — that is the `mic-capture-released` check.)
60	
61	## Endpointing is unreliable — plan for the miss
62	
63	Chrome decides on its own when an utterance ended, and it does get it wrong: interim hypotheses
64	keep arriving and no final result ever lands. Left alone the user repeats themselves and you get
65	`"heart heart"`. The fix is a pause monitor that discards the half-heard input and reopens a
66	fresh cycle — with interim results used **only** as the "still speaking" signal, never delivered
67	to the caller. (That last half is the `stt-interim-results-gated` check; the monitor itself, and
68	the window below, are yours.)
69	
70	Tune the window from real sessions, not from taste: 1.2 s cut real commands off solvers who
71	paused to think mid-instruction; 1.8 s keeps only the genuine missed-endpoint case. Anything
72	that ships an audible cue for the reset needs the same care — it fires often.
73	
74	## Contextual biasing exists only on the on-device path
75	
76	`SpeechRecognitionPhrase` / `processLocally` work only where Chrome has an on-device model.
77	Treat biasing as strictly best-effort:
78	
79	- probe availability **once** and memoize the promise;
80	- accept only the literal `'available'` — never trigger a language-pack download;
81	- apply phrases inside a `try` and fall through to un-biased recognition on any failure;
82	- keep the un-biased path byte-for-byte unchanged (don't make every caller await a probe it
83	  doesn't need).
84	
85	## Voices load lazily, and the default one is usually the worst
86	
87	`getVoices()` returning an empty list means *"not ready yet"*, not *"no voices"* — resolve the
88	voice on first speak and, on an empty list, use the default and try again next time rather than
89	caching the empty answer. The OS default is often the most robotic voice installed, so carry an
90	ordered preference list and take the first installed match. That list is **taste, and taste has
91	been wrong here before** (`Google US English` led it, sounded bad, and was demoted): treat both
92	the voice order and the speaking rate as user-facing settings with a modest default, not as
93	constants to tune once.
94	
95	## Give recognition errors a taxonomy
96	
97	Map the raw Web Speech error names onto a small named set the dialog policy can reason about,
98	and keep the mapping in one place. The policy cares about *kinds* — nothing heard, the mic was
99	refused, we aborted on purpose, the network went — not about spellings, and a `default → other`
100	arm means a browser inventing a new name degrades instead of crashing. (That the mapping is
101	total is the `stt-error-map-has-default` check; choosing the kinds, and keeping them in one
102	place, is not.) Log the codes short (`en`/`ed`/`ea`…) so a whole session fits in a diagnostics
103	dump.
104	########## .claudinite/local/packs/host-page-adaptation/RULES.md
105	# Adapting to a host page — the judgment core
106	
107	Working inside a web app you do not own: reading its DOM, driving it with synthetic input,
108	watching it change, and putting your own UI into its chrome. The mechanical rules — that a
109	page observer is disconnected, that a synthetic input event bubbles — are this pack's two
110	checks; what follows is only what no check can decide for you.
111	
112	Each rule below is a judgment about being a guest in someone else's page, and holds for any
113	code that does it — a userscript, an automation layer, an extension's content script. Where
114	one cites this repo — a file, a requirement id, a date — that is the **evidence** it was drawn
115	from, not the scope it applies to.
116	
117	The premise underneath all of it: **the host will change its markup without telling you, and
118	your code will not throw when it does.** A selector that matches nothing returns null; a click
119	on a renamed button never happens. Every rule here is about making that failure loud, local,
120	and cheap to fix.
121	
122	## Quarantine the host's DOM knowledge in one module
123	
124	All of it, behind an interface expressed in your own vocabulary — here `page-adapter/` returns
125	a `Snapshot` and takes `enterAnswer`, and the crossword model, the dialog policy and the
126	matcher never learn that the page exists (REQ-PAGE-011, `dev/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` §2). Two
127	things follow, and both are worth the discipline:
128	
129	- A redesign is a **one-directory** change, and the blast radius is knowable before you start.
130	- The rest of the codebase becomes testable without a browser at all — the pure layers here
131	  (`puzzle-model/`, `matching/`, `conversation/`) are pure *because* the quarantine holds.
132	
133	Inside that module, put **every selector and class string in one file**, and change values only
134	there (`page-adapter/selectors.js`). A selector inlined at its use site is the one that gets
135	missed when the host renames a class.
136	
137	Enforce the quarantine mechanically, by token: the repo's arch test fails if the host's class
138	prefix (`xwd__`) appears in code outside `page-adapter/`.
139	
140	## Identify host UI by a net, not by a selector
141	
142	A single selector is a bet that one class name survives. Cast a net instead, and make the last
143	strand semantic:
144	
145	- class nets that accept a family (`[class*="xwd__toolbar"]`), not one exact name;
146	- attribute and role hooks the host is less likely to churn (`role="cell"`, `data-testid`,
147	  `aria-label`);
148	- and a **text/shape fallback** underneath: the splash is found by class net *or* by "a visible
149	  container whose text says 'Ready to start solving' with a Play-ish button in it, whatever its
150	  classes are called" (`page-adapter/splash.js`); the pause veil is found by its copy plus
151	  visibility (`reader.js isPaused`).
152	
153	Visibility is part of identity. Hosts keep dismissed modals in the DOM, so a match that ignores
154	`display`/`visibility`/zero-size will keep reporting a splash you already cleared.
155	
156	## Write down what you verified the selectors against, and when
157	
158	The selectors file is the only place in the codebase whose truth lives on someone else's
159	server, so it carries its own provenance: the date and page it was last verified against, the
160	captured markup it was read from, and — most valuable — the **negative** findings.
161	`selectors.js` records that the state classes sit on the `<rect>` and not the `<g>`, that the
162	pencil button exposes no `aria-pressed` and no class change, that the letter/number `<text>`
163	nodes carry no distinguishing classes and the class-based selectors match nothing live. Each of
164	those is an hour of somebody's life, and none of it is recoverable from the code.
165	
166	## Ship a probe, and make a broken page a finding rather than an exception
167	
168	One entry point that reports the health of every selector against the live page —
169	`page-adapter/probe.js`, REQ-PAGE-009, run from the in-page menu (MT-01). It is the first thing
170	to run when a user says "it stopped working", and it turns "the extension is broken" into "the
171	clue-list wrapper selector matches 0, want 2".
172	
173	It must **never throw**: a probe that dies on the first missing element reports one fault and
174	hides the other nine. Collect a row per selector and return them all — and have it capture
175	forensics for the things you could *not* read (the probe here dumps the pencil button's
176	attributes precisely because its ON state has never been readable), so the next report arrives
177	with the evidence already in it.
178	
179	## Mirror the host in a fixture, and let the fixture define the expected shape
180	
181	A saved, simplified copy of the host page (`extension-test/fixtures/fake-nyt/`, served by
182	`npm run fixture`) mirrors the selectors exactly, and the integration tests drive that. It buys
183	two things a live page cannot: the read/write/watch cycle is testable in CI at all, and the
184	whole voice loop is rehearsable locally without a subscription (`npm run build:dev` widens the
185	matches to `localhost:8787`, MT-23).
186	
187	Its limit is the same as its virtue — **the fixture only ever shows you the markup you already
188	knew about**, so a passing suite is never evidence about the live page. Keep a manual-test
189	document for what only the real host can answer (`dev/docs/MANUAL-TESTS.md`), and treat every
190	live finding as a fixture update.
191	
192	## Never trust a write — verify by re-reading
193	
194	Address the target by position rather than relying on the host's own cursor conventions (click
195	each cell, then type one letter — immune to the host's advance-on-type and skip-filled
196	settings), then **read the DOM back and confirm what you meant is there** (REQ-PAGE-007). The
197	host may ignore untrusted events, may auto-advance differently than you assumed, may reject the
198	input silently; the re-read is the only thing that distinguishes those from success.
199	
200	Poll the re-read, don't do it synchronously after the last dispatch: the host renders
201	asynchronously (React here), so the DOM immediately after your event is the DOM *before* the
202	app processed it. And aim your events at a node **inside the app's own subtree** — the selected
203	element if it has focus, otherwise a known app node. A modern app delegates key handling near
204	its root, which is a descendant of `<body>`, so an event dispatched at `document` or `body`
205	bubbles *past* it and is never seen (`page-adapter/writer.js`).
206	
207	## A synthetic keystroke must carry the fields a real one would
208	
209	The browser fills in the deprecated `keyCode`/`which`/`charCode` on every real keystroke; on
210	a synthetic one they are plain init fields that default to 0, so
211	`new KeyboardEvent('keydown', { key: 'A' })` reaches the page as a keystroke whose keyCode is
212	0. Deprecated is not the same as unread: hosts with a long-lived key-handling layer still
213	branch on the legacy fields — this one does (verified live, MT-02) — and a 0 matches nothing,
214	so the handler runs and nothing happens, indistinguishable from "the app ignores untrusted
215	events". Mirror the real event instead: `keyCode` and `which` alongside `key`/`code`,
216	`charCode` on `keypress`, and the full keydown → keypress → keyup sequence a real keystroke
217	produces (`page-adapter/writer.js` `keyEventInit`/`typeKey`).
218	
219	Build the init in **one helper** and spread it at the single dispatch site, so fidelity is one
220	function's job. That factoring is also why this rule is prose rather than a check: the init a
221	well-factored adapter dispatches is opaque to a static scan (`{ ...init }` could carry
222	anything), so a check here could only ever police code that bypasses the helper — and the
223	mistake in that code is bypassing the helper, not the field it then forgot.
224	
225	## Put back any host state you borrowed, and degrade when you cannot read it
226	
227	Driving a host toggle means driving it back: pencil mode is set to match the write and restored
228	afterwards, so the user's own typing mode is never stolen (REQ-PAGE-012).
229	
230	You will often be unable to read the state you are toggling — the live pencil button has no
231	`aria-pressed` and no class change, so "on or off?" is genuinely unanswerable. Design for the
232	unreadable case as the **normal** one, not the error case: fall back to click parity, and let
233	the feature that depends on it degrade (the letters still land; only the pencil softening is
234	lost, REQ-ANS-019) rather than failing the operation.
235	
236	## The host has a lifecycle of its own, and its blank states are not your user's doing
237	
238	You are sharing the page with an app that has its own timers, veils and modals, and each one
239	looks like something else from inside your adapter:
240	
241	- **Idle timers.** This host auto-pauses a quiet puzzle after ~30 s of no keyboard input. A
242	  voice solver touches no keyboard, so the adapter sends a bare `Shift` keydown/keyup on every
243	  heard command — a real key event that types nothing and moves nothing (REQ-LIFE-017). Choose
244	  the nudge so it cannot mutate state, and drive it from real user activity, never from a timer
245	  of your own: when the user really has gone quiet, the host *should* pause and your session
246	  should end with it.
247	- **Veils that blank the content.** The pause veil empties the visible entries. A change watcher
248	  that diffs first and checks for the veil second will read that as the user clearing the whole
249	  grid. Check for the host's own overlay states **before** diffing, report the state once, and
250	  return (`page-adapter/watcher.js`).
251	- **Pre-content splashes.** The board may not exist for minutes while a "Ready to start
252	  solving?" modal is up. Absence of the content is not absence of the app.
253	
254	## Be inert when you are off
255	
256	Your code loads on the host's page whether or not the user is using you, so **doing nothing is
257	the resting state** (REQ-NFR-004). Watchers are created on demand and stopped with the session;
258	nothing polls; nothing observes between sessions.
259	
260	Keep load-time page changes to an explicit, minimal carve-out — here exactly one: mounting the
261	toolbar button (REQ-LIFE-012). Mount it by waiting with a `MutationObserver` that **disconnects
262	the moment the element lands** (the `page-observers-disconnected` check), and give up only when
263	the host shows no app markup at all — a slow render or a splash must not cost you the button,
264	but an archive page must not leave you waiting forever.
265	########## .claudinite/local/packs/browser-speech/README.md
266	# browser-speech pack (local)
267	
268	A pack for the **browser speech surfaces**: `SpeechRecognition` / `webkitSpeechRecognition`,
269	`chrome.tts`, `speechSynthesis`, and the microphone capture behind them. Declared by hand as
270	`local/browser-speech` in `.claudinite-checks.json`.
271	
272	**Every rule judges a browser API contract, not a product decision.** Each one holds in any
273	voice-driven web app — nothing in a rule's logic, rationale, or fix text is specific to this
274	repo, and the scan is repo-shape agnostic (see below), so the pack cannot pass vacuously green
275	somewhere laid out differently. This repo is where the rules were *discovered* and is the corpus
276	they are verified against; it is not what they are about.
277	
278	**Why local, not a canon declaration:** the mounted canon shelf has no home for this facet. The
279	`chrome-extension` pack covers MV3 build/runtime gotchas and says nothing about speech;
280	`chrome-extension-release`, `node`, `github-actions`, `tidy-repo`, `spec-driven-product` and
281	`executable-requirements` are all orthogonal. Nothing here duplicates a canon rule.
282	
283	**Provenance:** distilled from this repo's real usage — `extension/src/speech/` (`stt-port.js`,
284	`tts-port.js`, `remote-tts-port.js`, `biasing.js`), the sequential action loop in
285	`extension/src/app/orchestrator.js`, decisions D2 and D11 in `dev/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, the
286	`aec`/`od` diagnostics in `dev/docs/SESSION-LOG.md`, and the mic-teardown live check in issue
287	\#63. Nothing in it is invented.
288	
289	**Promotion note:** the checks are written to be lifted as-is — repo-shape agnostic scan, API
290	contracts only, no project identifiers in any rule's logic or messages — so the central promote
291	stage should be able to move them into a canon `browser-speech` (or `web-speech`) technology pack
292	with only the `doc:` paths rewritten. The `RULES.md` prose is the part still worth re-reading for
293	project coupling at promote time: some of it records tuning this product measured (the pause
294	window) rather than a fact of the API. Until then it lives here.
295	
296	## Checks
297	
298	| Check | Enforces (≤5 words) | Severity |
299	|---|---|---|
300	| `tts-speak-settles` | speak settles on every outcome | blocking |
301	| `stt-terminal-handlers` | recognizer wires onend and onerror | blocking |
302	| `mic-capture-released` | getUserMedia capture stops its tracks | blocking |
303	| `mic-constraints-not-screen-capture` | mic constraints exclude display-only ones | blocking |
304	| `stt-error-map-has-default` | error mapping has a catch-all | blocking |
305	| `stt-interim-results-gated` | interim results gated on isFinal | blocking |
306	
307	**Scope.** All six scan any browser source file (`.js/.mjs/.cjs/.ts/.tsx/.jsx`) except test and
308	vendor paths — never a hard-coded project root. Each rule is already gated on the speech API it
309	judges actually appearing in the file, so the API usage *is* the trigger and the scan can be
310	repo-shaped; a path scope wired to one layout would make every rule match zero files and pass
311	vacuously green elsewhere, which is the worst failure mode a check has. The exclusion that
312	matters — test scaffolding, whose hand-rolled speech fakes implement only the halves of a
313	contract a given case needs — is stated directly, by test/vendor path and test filename.
314	
315	**Parsed, not grepped, where the name alone doesn't decide it.**
316	`mic-constraints-not-screen-capture` judges `suppressLocalAudioPlayback` / `restrictOwnAudio` only
317	where they *reach* a microphone capture — the balanced argument list of a `getUserMedia(` call,
318	plus one hop into a same-file constant that list names (hoisting constraints into a frozen
319	constant is how real code writes them). Every other use of those names is legitimate: a real
320	`getDisplayMedia` call, a `getSupportedConstraints()` probe, a comment explaining the trap — all
321	of which a file-wide grep would false-alarm on, this repo's own `stt-port.js` included.
322	
323	`stt-error-map-has-default` reads a switch's arms at the switch body's *own* brace depth, so a
324	nested switch's `default:` is not mistaken for the outer mapping's catch-all — and it treats a
325	`return`/`throw` immediately after the switch as the catch-all it is, since that is the other
326	idiomatic way to write a total mapping. It judges only switches whose arms `return` a kind: a
327	switch dispatching side effects over error names is a different shape, and the rule has no
328	honest opinion about its missing arm.
329	
330	`stt-interim-results-gated` reads the *value* assigned to `interimResults` rather than the name:
331	an explicit `= false` turns the flag off, every result is then final, and there is nothing to
332	gate — while a computed flag (`rec.interimResults = pauseResetMs > 0`, the shape real code takes)
333	counts as on, since a check cannot show it is off and the handler has to survive it being true.
334	It also judges only a file that spells its result handler out: a config module that sets the flag
335	and hands the recognizer on, and `rec.onresult = this.handleResult`, both keep their gate in a
336	file this check is not looking at, so delegation is answered with silence rather than a guess.
337	
338	**Both DOM wiring forms count.** `el.onend = …` and `el.addEventListener('end', …)` are equally
339	correct, so every handler rule accepts either (`lib.mjs` `wires`). A rule that knew only the
340	property form would silently pass half the world's code and false-alarm on any file mixing the
341	two.
342	
343	Red-first fixtures live in `pack.test.mjs`: each rule is run against a violating source and a
344	clean one — in both wiring forms, and in TypeScript under a plain `src/` as well as JavaScript —
345	and then against this repo's real `extension/src/` tree, which must stay quiet. The project's
346	vitest run picks the file up via the `.claudinite/local/packs/**/*.test.mjs` include in
347	`vitest.config.js`, so the checks ship green in CI.
348	
349	**When a check's whole point is precision, red-first has to prove it in two directions.** A
350	violating fixture failing and a clean one passing only proves the shipped check is correct — it
351	says nothing about whether the parsing it does was *necessary*. Also run the quiet fixtures
352	against the naive alternative the parsing exists to avoid (here: a file-wide grep in place of the
353	`getUserMedia(` scoping) and confirm they'd wrongly fire — that's what earns the parsing its
354	complexity. `mic-constraints-not-screen-capture`'s fixtures do both: the three firing fixtures
355	fail with the rule neutered, and the three quiet fixtures — plus this repo's own `stt-port.js` —
356	fail against a naive whole-file grep. `stt-error-map-has-default`'s do the same: its three firing
357	fixtures fail with the rule neutered, and against a naive "≥2 error names and no `default:`
358	anywhere in the file" grep the trailing-`return`, side-effect-dispatch and comment-only fixtures
359	all wrongly fire while the nested-switch violation goes undetected.
360	`stt-interim-results-gated`'s do the same: with its `isFinal` gate neutered both the clean fixture
361	*and this repo's own `stt-port.js`* fire — which is what proves the rule reaches the real file
362	rather than passing over it — and against a naive "mentions `interimResults`, never `isFinal`"
363	grep the flag-off, config-module, delegated-handler and comment-only fixtures all wrongly fire.
364	
365	## Prose (`RULES.md`)
366	
367	| Rule (≤5 words) | How enforced |
368	|---|---|
369	| chrome.tts unavailable to content scripts | prose |
370	| recognizer takes no audio constraints | prose (its display-only-constraint trap is checked) |
371	| preflight the mic deliberately | prose |
372	| endpointing fails; monitor mid-utterance pauses | prose (that interim results aren't delivered is checked) |
373	| biasing is on-device only | prose |
374	| voices load lazily; default is worst | prose |
375	| map speech errors to a taxonomy | prose (that the mapping is total is checked) |
376	########## .claudinite/local/packs/host-page-adaptation/README.md
377	# host-page-adaptation pack (local)
378	
379	A pack for **being a guest in a web app you do not own**: reading its DOM, driving it with
380	synthetic input, watching it change, injecting your own UI into its chrome, and surviving the
381	day it is redesigned. Declared by hand as `local/host-page-adaptation` in
382	`.claudinite-checks.json`.
383	
384	**Every rule judges a DOM/API contract, not a product decision.** Each one holds for any code
385	driving a third-party page — a userscript, a browser-automation layer, an extension's content
386	script — and nothing in a rule's logic, rationale or fix text is specific to this repo. The scan
387	is repo-shape agnostic (see below), so the pack cannot pass vacuously green somewhere laid out
388	differently. This repo is where the rules were *discovered* and is the corpus they are verified
389	against; it is not what they are about.
390	
391	**Why local, not a canon declaration:** the mounted canon shelf has no home for this facet. The
392	`chrome-extension` pack covers MV3 *mechanics* — manifest, permissions, how a content script is
393	registered and why it can't be an ES module — i.e. how your code reaches the page; it says
394	nothing about what to do once it is there. `chrome-extension-release`, `node`,
395	`github-actions`, `tidy-repo`, `spec-driven-product`, `executable-requirements` and `barriers`
396	are orthogonal, and the sibling local pack `browser-speech` owns the speech surfaces, not the
397	page. Nothing here duplicates a canon rule.
398	
399	**Provenance:** distilled from this repo's real usage — the whole of
400	`extension/src/page-adapter/` (`selectors.js`, `reader.js`, `writer.js`, `watcher.js`,
401	`probe.js`, `splash.js`, `session-button.js`), the REQ-PAGE and REQ-LIFE requirement families
402	in `dev/docs/REQUIREMENTS.md`, the quarantine rule REQ-PAGE-011 and its arch test
403	(`extension-test/unit/arch.test.js`), the live-page findings recorded in `writer.js` (MT-02) and
404	in `selectors.js`'s dated verification notes, and the fake-host fixture
405	(`extension-test/fixtures/fake-nyt/`). Nothing in it is invented.
406	
407	**Promotion note:** the checks are written to be lifted as-is — repo-shape agnostic scan, DOM
408	contracts only, no project identifiers in any rule's logic or messages — so the central promote
409	stage should be able to move them into a canon pack for this facet (`host-page-adaptation`, or
410	whatever a canon `html`/DOM pack calls it) with only the `doc:` paths rewritten. The `RULES.md`
411	prose is the part still worth re-reading for project coupling at promote time: several rules
412	cite this host's specific behaviours (the ~30 s idle auto-pause, the pencil button with no
413	readable state) as evidence, and those are examples of a category, not constants.
414	
415	## Checks
416	
417	| Check | Enforces (≤5 words) | Severity |
418	|---|---|---|
419	| `page-observers-disconnected` | started DOM observers get disconnected | blocking |
420	| `synthetic-input-events-bubble` | dispatched input events set bubbles | blocking |
421	
422	**Scope.** Both scan any browser source file (`.js/.mjs/.cjs/.ts/.tsx/.jsx`) except test
423	and vendor paths — never a hard-coded project root. Each rule is gated on the DOM API it judges
424	actually appearing in the file, so the API usage *is* the trigger and the scan can be
425	repo-shaped; a path scope wired to one layout would make every rule match zero files and pass
426	vacuously green elsewhere, which is the worst failure mode a check has. The exclusion that
427	matters is test scaffolding: a test dispatching a bare event at its own jsdom node, or spinning
428	an observer it lets the runner collect, is doing something purpose-built and is not adapting to
429	a host page.
430	
431	**Parsed, not grepped, where the name alone doesn't decide it.**
432	
433	`synthetic-input-events-bubble` judges only events that are actually **dispatched** (a probe
434	event constructed to feature-detect is not input), only the interfaces that model **real user
435	input** (a `CustomEvent` is your own signal to your own listener and is legitimately
436	non-bubbling), and it resolves each side of the dispatch through **one hop**: the constructor
437	through an alias (`const Ctor = isKey ? view.KeyboardEvent : view.MouseEvent` is how a generic
438	`fire()` helper is written, and this repo's single dispatch site is exactly that shape), and
439	the dispatched value through a local (`const ev = new MouseEvent('click');
440	el.dispatchEvent(ev)` is the other shape real dispatch code takes). An init that spreads
441	(`{ ...init }`) without an explicit `bubbles:` is beyond what the rule can see, so it stays
442	silent there: the caller may well set the field, and a check that guessed would false-alarm on
443	precisely the well-factored helper that centralises this.
444	
445	**A third check was cut at review.** `synthetic-key-events-legacy-fields` (a synthetic
446	`KeyboardEvent` init must carry `keyCode`/`which`) enforced a real live-page lesson (MT-02) —
447	but this repo's only key-event construction builds its init in a helper and spreads it at the
448	one dispatch site, exactly the shape a spread-silent check can never read. A check that is
449	structurally blind to the house pattern can only ever fire on code that bypasses the `fire()`
450	helper, and the mistake in that code is the bypass, not the field it then forgot. The lesson
451	lands as prose instead (`RULES.md`, "A synthetic keystroke must carry the fields a real one
452	would").
453	
454	`page-observers-disconnected` is deliberately **file-scoped, not flow-scoped**: proving a
455	particular observer is disconnected on every path needs real data-flow analysis, and a check
456	that guesses is worse than one that asks a simple, honest question — "this file starts an
457	observer on the page; does it anywhere disconnect one?". An observer constructed but never
458	`.observe(`d has started nothing and is not asked.
459	
460	Red-first fixtures live in `pack.test.mjs`: each rule is run against violating sources and
461	clean ones — in both the direct and the aliased-constructor form, in TypeScript under a plain
462	`src/` as well as JavaScript — and then against this repo's real `extension/src/` tree, which
463	must stay quiet. The project's vitest run picks the file up via the
464	`.claudinite/local/packs/**/*.test.mjs` include in `vitest.config.js`, so the checks ship green
465	in CI.
466	
467	**When a check's whole point is precision, red-first has to prove it in two directions.** A
468	violating fixture failing and a clean one passing only proves the shipped check is correct — it
469	says nothing about whether the parsing it does was *necessary*. So the quiet fixtures are also
470	run against the naive alternative each piece of parsing exists to avoid, and confirmed to fire
471	there: a whole-file `new …Event(` grep wrongly flags the `CustomEvent`, never-dispatched and
472	already-bubbling cases.
473	
474	## Prose (`RULES.md`)
475	
476	| Rule (≤5 words) | How enforced |
477	|---|---|
478	| quarantine host DOM in one module | prose |
479	| identify host UI by nets | prose |
480	| date what selectors were verified against | prose |
481	| probe reports, never throws | prose |
482	| mirror the host in a fixture | prose |
483	| never trust a write; re-read | prose |
484	| synthetic keystrokes carry real-event fields | prose (its bubbles half is checked) |
485	| restore borrowed host state; degrade | prose |
486	| host lifecycle states aren't user actions | prose |
487	| be inert when off | prose (its observer teardown is checked) |

494	import sttInterimResultsGated from './stt-interim-results-gated.mjs';
495	
496	// browser-speech — driving the browser's speech APIs (SpeechRecognition /
497	// webkitSpeechRecognition, chrome.tts, speechSynthesis, and the getUserMedia
498	// capture behind them).

505	// gotchas and says nothing about speech, and `node` / `github-actions` /

content.content:
3:description: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
8:Portable practices for writing tests you can actually trust — proving a test fails before relying on it, snapshot/golden discipline, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, and how to gate a fuzzy quality metric. These are project-agnostic; a consuming repo's own test *mechanics* (runner, layout, which suites exist) stay in its own docs. (General software-engineering practices live in [the basics pack's RULES.md](../../RULES.md); CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha live in [the git-github-advanced skill](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md).)
20:- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
21:- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
22:- Run a suite you know is slow as **its own command with an explicit timeout well above its measured runtime**, and do the dependency install as a *separate, earlier* call. An agent shell caps a command at a default (order of a couple of minutes) and pushes it to the background when it expires; the reflex is then to start the suite over, so one green result costs double the wall clock with two suites racing each other. Chaining setup in front of the suite is what usually pushes the pair past the cap. If a run does get backgrounded, wait on the one already running rather than launching a second.
23:- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically. (The SPA-render fallback's CI test renders a `data:` URL whose script fills an empty root, not a real SPA — #310.)
29:- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
